(C) Certain firearm offenses Any alien who at any time after admission is convicted under any law of purchasing, selling, offering for sale, exchanging, using, owning, possessing, or carrying, or of attempting or conspiring to purchase, sell, offer for sale, exchange, use, own, possess, or carry, any weapon, part, or accessory which is a firearm or destructive device (as defined in section 921(a) of title 18) in violation of any law is deportable. (D) Miscellaneous crimes Any alien who at any time has been convicted (the judgment on such conviction becoming final) of, or has been so convicted of a conspiracy or attempt to violate— (i) any offense under chapter 37 (relating to espionage), chapter 105 (relating to sabotage), or chapter 115 (relating to treason and sedition) of title 18 for which a term of imprisonment of five or more years may be imposed; (ii) any offense under section 871 or 960 of title 18; (iii) a violation of any provision of the Military Selective Service Act (50 U.S.C. App. 451 et seq.) [now 50 U.S.C. 3801 et seq.] or the Trading With the Enemy Act (50 U.S.C. App. 1 et seq.) [now 50 U.S.C. 4301 et seq.]; or (iv) a violation of section 1185 or 1328 of this title, is deportable. (E) Crimes of domestic violence, stalking, or violation of protection order, crimes against children and (i) Domestic violence, stalking, and child abuse Any alien who at any time after admission is convicted of a crime of domestic violence, a crime of stalking, or a crime of child abuse, child neglect, or child abandonment is deportable. For purposes of this clause, the term "crime of domestic violence" means any crime of violence (as defined in section 16 of title 18) against a person committed by a current or former spouse of the person, by an individual with whom the person shares a child in common, by an individual who is cohabiting with or has cohabited with the person as a spouse, by an individual similarly situated to a spouse of the person under the domestic or family violence laws of the jurisdiction where the offense occurs, or by any other individual against a person who is protected from that individual's acts under the domestic or family violence laws of the United States or any State, Indian tribal government, or unit of local government. (ii) Violators of protection orders Any alien who at any time after admission is enjoined under a protection order issued by a court and whom the court determines has engaged in conduct that violates the portion of a protection order that involves protection against credible threats of violence, repeated harassment, or bodily injury to the person or persons for whom the protection order was issued is deportable. For purposes of this clause, the term "protection order" means any injunction issued for the purpose of preventing violent or threatening acts of domestic violence, including temporary or final orders issued by civil or criminal courts (other than support or child custody orders or provisions) whether obtained by filing an independent action or as a pendente lite order in another proceeding. (F) Trafficking Any alien described in section 1182(a)(2)(H) of this title is deportable. 

(7) Waiver for victims of domestic violence (A) In general The Attorney General is not limited by the criminal court record and may waive the application of paragraph (2)(E)(i) (with respect to crimes of domestic violence and crimes of stalking) and (ii) in the case of an alien who has been battered or subjected to extreme cruelty and who is not and was not the primary perpetrator of violence in the relationship— (i) 1 upon a determination that— (I) the alien was acting is 2 self-defense; (II) the alien was found to have violated a protection order intended to protect the alien; or (III) the alien committed, was arrested for, was convicted of, or pled guilty to committing a crime— (aa) that did not result in serious bodily injury; and (bb) where there was a connection between the crime and the alien's having been battered or subjected to extreme cruelty. (B) Credible evidence considered In acting on applications under this paragraph, the Attorney General shall consider any credible evidence relevant to the application. The determination of what evidence is credible and the weight to be given that evidence shall be within the sole discretion of the Attorney General.

actions.short_description: H.R.275 monthly specified-alien encounter reports
actions.compact_description: H.R.275 would require monthly public/congressional DHS reports on specified potential-security-risk alien encounters, including nationality/residence, geography and port/between-port/interior distinctions, plus an initial historical-period report.
actions.meaning: The exact H.R.275 EH proposal requires the DHS Secretary, by the seventh day of each month starting with the first full month after enactment, to publish a DHS webpage report and submit it to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees. Each report must give the preceding month's total encounters of “special interest aliens”, their nationalities or countries of last habitual residence, geographic disaggregation, whether encounters occurred at land/air/sea ports of entry, between ports or in the U.S. interior, and identification of covered-nation nationalities/residences. The first report also covers January 20, 2021 through January 19, 2025. The operative definition is an INA-defined alien who, based on analysis of travel patterns, potentially poses a national-security risk to the United States or its interests. It does not establish an actual threat, criminal guilt, inadmissibility or removal for an individual. The incorporated covered nations are North Korea, China, Russia and Iran under 10 USC 4872(f)(2); only that definition is imported, not the unrelated procurement powers. The operative report covers DHS encounters, including the interior. The title's reference to attempts at unlawful entry does not create an unstated unlawful-entry-only reporting limit. This bill adds this specific recurring and retrospective reporting duty; it neither changes admission/removal eligibility nor authorizes new detention or spending. No actual report, encounter totals, threat finding or enactment is inferred.
limitations: The deadline is the seventh day of each month beginning with the first full post-enactment month, for the immediately preceding month. The first report additionally covers the fixed January 20, 2021–January 19, 2025 historical period.

The reported category depends on travel-pattern analysis and potential security risk, not proof of guilt or actual threat. The INA alien definition excludes U.S. citizens/nationals. Covered-nation labeling reports four incorporated countries rather than creating admission sanctions.

The exact operative scope includes ports, between-port encounters and interior encounters; unlawful attempted entry is not stated as an additional predicate in section 2(a). A measure title cannot narrow that scope.

This is reporting/publication legislation, not actual enforcement, new detention or admission/removal eligibility. Whole-bill passage does not establish separate preferences about each data category, actual encounter numbers or enactment.

R. 275 _______________________________________________________________________ AN ACT To require the Secretary of Homeland Security to publish on a monthly basis the number of special interest aliens encountered attempting to unlawfully enter the United States, and for other purposes. Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the ``Special Interest Alien Reporting Act of 2025''. SEC. 2. PUBLICATION BY THE DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY OF THE NUMBER OF SPECIAL INTEREST ALIENS ENCOUNTERED. (a) In General.--Not later than the seventh day of each month beginning with the first full month that begins after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of Homeland Security shall publish on a publicly available webpage of the Department of Homeland Security and submit to the Committee on Homeland Security of the House of Representatives and the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs of the Senate a report on the total number, and an identification of the nationalities or countries of last habitual residence, of special interest aliens encountered by the Department during the immediately preceding month. Each such report shall also include the following: (1) Such number disaggregated by geographic regions of such encounters. (2) Specifications relating to whether such encounters were made at land, air, or sea ports of entry, between ports of entry, or in the interior of the United States. (3) Identification of any such nationalities or countries of last habitual residence that are covered nations. (b) Inclusion.--The first report required under subsection (a) shall also include the matters described in such subsection for the time period from January 20, 2021, through January 19, 2025. (c) Definitions.--In this section: (1) Alien.--The term ``alien'' has the meaning given such term in section 101 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101). (2) Covered nation.--The term ``covered nation'' has the meaning given such term in section 4872(f)(2) of title 10, United States Code. (3) Special interest alien.--The term ``special interest alien'' means an alien who, based on an analysis of travel patterns, potentially poses a national security risk to the United States or its interests. actions.short_description: H.R.1 Senate replacement: selected border, detention and asylum, employment-authorization and selected sponsor/enforcement fees
actions.compact_description: Selected Senate H.R. 1 provisions would fund border infrastructure and detention, set fiscal 2025 asylum filing/pending fee floors of $100 each and specified asylum/parole/TPS employment-authorization initial/renewal fee floors of $550/$275, with distinct duration and termination rules. This is a whole-replacement concurrence choice, with qualifications.
actions.meaning:
This July3 House concurrence concerns the Senate's July1 EAS, which strikes all after the first word and replaces the earlier H.R.1 text. It is the complete multi-domain reconciliation replacement, not a second passage of the unchanged House bill or a separate vote on its Immigration components. Selected Immigration highlights here concern border infrastructure, detention and asylum fees; other immigration-related benefits, taxes, employment authorization, child-sponsor, reimbursement and enforcement provisions are not exhaustively described. Section90001 would appropriate an additional $46.55billion for fiscal2025 to CBP, available until September30,2029, for new/replacement primary, waterborne and secondary barriers, access roads, detection attributes and ground preparation for CBP operations and barrier construction/maintenance. The different House60001 accounts are not silently used to define this replacement amount or its purposes. Section90003 would appropriate an additional $45billion for fiscal2025 to ICE, available until September30,2029, for single-adult alien detention and family residential-center capacity. Aliens MAY be detained at family centers pending an INA removal decision and, if ordered removed, until removal. Single-adult detention standards are set in the Secretary's discretion CONSISTENT WITH APPLICABLE LAW. The family-center definition covers apprehended/encountered family units, including children who are not statutorily defined unaccompanied alien children, and does not reproduce the House's express regardless-of-State-licensing clause.6USC279(g)(2) requires no lawful immigration status, under18 age, and no US parent/legal guardian or none available for care/physical custody. Neither the capacity funding nor permission establishes automatic detention/removal of every alien, elimination of all legal constraints or actual operations. Section100002 requires an additional fee upon filing an asylum application. The fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or the amount set by DHS/the Attorney General, as applicable, by rule; it cannot be waived/reduced. From fiscal2026 the prior fiscal-year fee is increased by the printed July-to-July CPI-U increment rounded down to a multiple of $10. Half of Attorney-General-filed receipts go to EOIR; half of DHS-filed receipts go to USCIS's existing Immigration Examinations Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; uncredited receipts go to Treasury. This $100 filing floor differs from the House's $1,000 floor. Section100009 separately requires an additional fee for EACH CALENDAR YEAR an asylum application remains pending. Its fiscal2025 amount is the greater of $100 or a DHS rule amount, followed by the printed CPI-U annual adjustment with the increment rounded DOWN TO THE NEAREST DOLLAR; receipts go to Treasury and the fee cannot be waived/reduced. Do not transfer that rounding to the initial-filing fee or back to the House's differently printed yearly formula. Section100018 changes pre-vote INA208(d)(3)/8USC1158(d)(3) from MAY impose fees to SHALL and replaces the following cost-cap/installment/nonmandatory-fee language with preserved additional adjudication/naturalization-fee authority under286(m). The baseline already authorized asylum-consideration, employment-authorization and asylum-based adjustment fees;1356(m)/(n) govern existing account/cost-recovery context. No first-ever fee authority, new asylum eligibility test from that edit, specific implemented collection rule or actual payment is inferred. Employment-authorization fees are separate from asylum filing and annual pending-application fees. Senate100003 requires additional initial application fees for asylum applicants under1158(d)(2), paroled aliens andTPS employment-authorization applicants under1254a(a)(1)(B). Each fiscal2025 floor is$550 or a higher DHS rule amount, with no waiver/reduction and fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. The asylum-initial subsection contains no House-style six-month duration sentence; it credits25percent of fees collected PURSUANT TO THIS SUBSECTION to USCIS's existing fee account, retained/expended without further appropriation with NOT LESS THAN50percent of the credited share for benefit-fraud detection/prevention, and sends the rest to Treasury. Parole/TPS initial fees go to Treasury; their initial authorizations last one year or the duration of parole/TPS respectively, whichever is shorter. Senate100010 and100012 set separate parole/TPS employment-authorization renewal/extension fiscal2025 fee floors of$275, possible higher DHS rule amounts and later CPI increments rounded down to$10. Each sends25percent to USCIS's existing fee account to retain/spend without further appropriation and the rest to Treasury; no waiver/reduction.100012 states one year or the duration of the designation ofTPS, whichever is shorter.100010 literally says employment authorization for each paroled alien, OR ANY RENEWAL OR EXTENSION OF SUCH PAROLE, shall be valid for one year or parole duration, whichever is shorter. Preserve this printed antecedent and leave its application unresolved; do not rewrite it into a new parole-eligibility rule or import House six-month text. Senate100011 imposes at least$275 for each asylum-based employment-authorization renewal/extension, with25percent credited to USCIS's existing fee account without further appropriation, the rest to Treasury and no waiver/reduction. It prints no annual CPI formula or House-style six-month limit. It retains the three termination points: immediately after asylum-officer denial unless referred to an immigration judge;30days after immigration-judge denial unless timely appealed to BIA; immediately after BIA denies an appeal of asylum denial. It does not reproduce the separate House70013(d) prohibition on later grants/renewals/extensions absent a FederalCourtOfAppeals remand. Absence of that House sentence does not establish unlimited permission or erase other law. The complete pre-vote1158(d)(2) already permits regulated asylum-based work authorization while denying entitlement and preserving a180day wait for applicants not otherwise eligible. Existing1254a(a)(1)(B)/(a)(2) authorizes employment throughout TPS. Document-validity clauses do not themselves terminate TPS, create first employment authority or establish individual eligibility. Existing1182(d)(5)(A)/(B) preserves case-by-case temporary humanitarian/significant-public-benefit parole subject to the printed statutory exceptions, including its refugee qualification and the distinction from admission; paying a fee does not supply parole or work permission. Senate100016 requires a fiscal2025 fee of at least$5,000, or a higher DHS rule amount, on an alien BOTH ordered removed in absentia under1229a(b)(5) AND subsequently arrested by ICE, with fiscal2026-onward CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. It does not apply if the order was rescinded under1229a(b)(5)(C).50percent goes to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account, retained/expended without further appropriation; the rest goes to Treasury. It expressly bars waiver/reduction. These fee conditions preserve the underlying notice/address/removability proof, rescission, exceptional-circumstances definition and motion-to-reopen stay in complete pre-vote1229a(b)(5)/(e) and1229(a); an actual order/arrest, new removal ground or denied legal review is not inferred. Senate100017 separately requires an additional fee from any INADMISSIBLE alien at the time the person is apprehended BETWEEN PORTS OF ENTRY. Its fiscal2025 floor is$5,000 or a higher DHS rule amount, with later CPI-U increments rounded down to$10. Unlike House70022, this operative sentence does not name CBP as the apprehending actor. It prints TWO proceeds clauses: subsection(c) sends50percent to ICE's Detention and Removal Office Fee Account for retention/spending without further appropriation and the remainder to Treasury; subsection(d) says ALL fees under the section go to Treasury. The exact EAS HTML and officialPDF pages827-828 both print these clauses. The candidate preserves the apparent allocation conflict and does not choose an operative distribution. No express no-waiver clause is printed in100017; do not import100016(e) or House70022(d), or infer that a waiver is available. These are exact between-port/inadmissibility and in-absentia-plus-ICE-arrest fee predicates, not all enforcement encounters or a fee-imposed finding that an alien actually met any predicate. Senate100004 adds a parole-entry fee with fiscal2025floor$1,000 or higher DHS rule amount, subsequent CPI-U increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. Its exceptions require the alien to establish the parole reason to DHS's satisfaction on an INDIVIDUAL,CASE-BY-CASE basis; its no-waiver clause expressly preserves those exceptions. The fee exceptions retain their actual predicates: a medical emergency with necessary treatment unavailable in the foreign state where the alien resides OR a life-threatening emergency with insufficient normal-visa time; the parent/legal guardian of such a medical-emergency MINOR; the alien needed in the US to donate an organ or tissue for transplant, with insufficient normal-visa time; a close family member in the United States whose death is imminent, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving while that person is alive; or seeking to attend a close family member's funeral, when normal visa processing would prevent arriving in the United States in time for it; an adopted child's urgent treatment needed before expected final adoption-related visa issuance while in the petitioner's legal custody; a LAWFUL INA245 adjustment applicant returning after temporary travel abroad; and a person returned to a contiguous country under235(b)(2)(C) paroled to attend the person's immigration hearing. The law-enforcement significant-public-benefit exception requires a DHS determination that significant public benefit has resulted or will result from the parole, BOTH assistance to the USGovernment AND presence required in that matter, PLUS at least one of inadmissibility, failure to meet nonimmigrant-admission eligibility, or insufficient normal-visa time; it is not every asserted public benefit. Senate exception9 instead requires that the alien HASBEENGRANTED the status of Cuban/Haitianentrant as defined inPL96-422Sec501(e). That complete definition distinguishes special Cuban/Haitianentrant-parole/subsequently-established special-status categories from OTHERCuban/Haitian nationals with the listed parole/no-other-status, removal-proceeding or pending-asylum alternatives AND no final,nonappealable,legally-enforceable removal order. Its status-at-assistance/services wording is preserved in the bound definition, not silently turned into proof of the fee-specific grant condition or a nationality-only exemption. Do not use the different House Cuba-residence/family-petition/program conjunction to define this replacement, or infer actual parole/fee exemption from nationality. Existing1182(d)(5) authority/statutory exceptions/non-admission distinction remain; paying or excepting a fee does not grant parole, admission or adjustment. Senate100005 requires an additional SIJapplication fee from ANYALIEN,PARENT,ORLEGALGUARDIAN of an alien applying under1101(a)(27)(J), with fiscal2025floor$250 or a higher DHS rule amount, later CPI increments rounded down to$10 and Treasury disposition. It does not print the House one-viable-parent fee predicate or the House express waiver bar; no waiver availability or separate cumulative charges on every named payer are inferred. Complete1101(a)(27)(J) retains the juvenile-court dependency/custody and1ORboth-parent nonviability findings, best-interest-against-return finding, DHSconsent, HHS-specific custody-jurisdiction consent and no derivative parentage rights. These fee provisions do not grant SIJstatus, import a UAC-under18 definition or alter those eligibility findings by themselves. Senate100006 edits EXISTING1254a(c)(1)(B) registration authority: it raises the statutory fee MAXIMUM from$50 to$500, subject to fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustments rounded down to$10. It leaves the existing AttorneyGeneral MAYrequire a REASONABLE registration fee language and separate work-document fee authority; this is not a mandatory universal$500charge, a$500minimum, the House conditional additional fee or the separate$550initial/$275renewal EADfees. The amendment adds Treasury disposition and no waiver/reduction of required fees. The existing appropriation-credit sentence is NOTEXPRESSLYSTRUCK in the printed edit and remains in redesignatedclause(i), alongside addedclause(iii) directing all fees under the subparagraph to Treasury. Preserve that apparent proceeds interaction for legal/application review rather than silently deleting the baseline sentence or choosing an implemented distribution. The proposed registration-cap change does not grant or end TPS, guarantee status eligibility, prove payment or establish an individual's outcome. Senate 100007 adds a visa-integrity fee payable by any alien issued a nonimmigrant visa at issuance, in addition to other authorized fees. The fiscal 2025 minimum is $250 or a higher DHS rule amount; subsequent July-to-July CPI-U increments are rounded down to the nearest dollar. Unreimbursed fees go to Treasury and the applicable fee cannot be waived or reduced. DHS MAY reimburse after the visa period of validity expires only if the alien demonstrates compliance with ALL visa conditions after admission, including no unauthorized employment, AND one of two printed alternatives: (A) did not seek to extend the period of admission during the visa validity period AND departed no later than five days after the last day of "such period"; OR (B) during that validity period WAS GRANTED an extension of nonimmigrant status or adjustment to lawful permanent resident status. The text uses "such period" in alternative (A); its application is reserved rather than silently choosing visa validity or authorized admission as the referent. The House nonuse, filing-only and change-of-status alternatives are not imported into this version. A filing is not a grant; reimbursement remains discretionary and conditional, not guaranteed repayment or a general permission to stay/work. The complete pre-vote 1101(a)(26) definition distinguishes proper nonimmigrant visa issuance from actual admission, compliance or an individual outcome. Senate 100008 separately adds an I-94 application fee on any alien submitting that application, with fiscal 2025 minimum $24 or higher DHS rule amount, later July-to-July CPI-U increments rounded down to the nearest dollar and no waiver/reduction. Twenty percent of collected fees goes to the existing Land Border Inspection Fee Account pursuant to 1356(q)(2), available to CBP to retain and spend without further appropriation for I-94 processing; amounts not deposited there go to Treasury. The complete pre-vote subsection (q) establishes the account and its land-port receipt/expense/report framework. That baseline account scope is not substituted for the new section's any-alien I-94 application predicate, and its appropriations refunds are not applicant reimbursements. The visa fee and I-94 fee have separate collection events and dispositions; neither proves actual admission, visa compliance, a collection or immigration-status outcome. Senate 100014 amends the existing ESTA fee components under complete pre-vote1187(h)(3): the existing $17 per travel authorization remains, the separate full-System-cost-recovery component gains a $10 MINIMUM while retaining that cost condition, and a new component is at least $13 PER TRAVEL AUTHORIZATION. This does not describe a $10 or $13 total or first creation of ESTA. Its sunset edit extends the clause(i)(I) Travel Promotion Fund fee restriction from fiscal years beginning after October31,2028 to those beginning after October31,2034; it is not a sunset of every component. Its fiscal2026-onward CPI-U adjustment names the clause(i)(II) amount but literally uses the prior fee required UNDER THIS SUBPARAGRAPH as its base. That component/base relationship remains a separate application question, not a silently substituted isolated cost component or definite whole-fee adjustment; no increment-rounding rule is printed. Unlike selected House70017, this section does not edit existing clause(ii) disposition language: that baseline directs (i)(I) to the Travel Promotion Fund and (i)(II) to Treasury for System administration, but does not assign newly added (i)(III) by name. The new $13 component's disposition is separately reserved, without copying the House Treasury sentence or claiming to have closed other package funding provisions. Exact officialPDFpages819-821 visually confirm the printed adjustment language and section boundary; no HTML-parser repair is made. Existing travel-eligibility/admissibility/visa-eligibility distinctions remain, and no express new ESTA fee-waiver prohibition or inferred waiver availability is imported from EVUS. Senate 100015 separately adds an EVUS fee at enrollment for any alien SUBJECT to that System, additional to other authorized fees, with fiscal2025 minimum $30 or a higher DHS rule amount, later CPI-U increments rounded down to $0.25 and no waiver/reduction. It inserts a new1356(w) CBP EVUS Account with deposits equal to fees received MINUS $5 multiplied by the NUMBER OF PAYMENTS collected; that same $5-times-payments amount goes to Treasury. This payment-count language is retained rather than substituted with House70019's per-enrollment wording or inferred one-payment-per-enrollment implementation. Account amounts are appropriated without further appropriation and available until expended for CBP EVUS administration costs. OfficialPDF823 confirms the payment-count basis. The fee does not expand who is subject to EVUS, establish admission or visa/status eligibility, prove compliance or document an actual payment. Senate 100013 adds ten EOIR fee provisions despite its narrower adjustment-of-status section title. In(a), an alien who files the specified adjustment application with immigration court OR whose application is adjudicated there pays at filing OR before court adjudication. In(b)/(c), the fee is required from any alien at court filing of the inadmissibility-waiver/TPS application OR before court adjudication. No automatic duplicate charge at both events is asserted. The(d)/(e) alien appeals, (f) practitioner appeal and(g) alien motion collect at filing. The(h) suspension application and(i) application for an alien who is a lawful permanent resident collect at court filing. Senate(j) separately requires a payer who IS NOT A LAWFUL PERMANENT RESIDENT at the time that payer files with immigration court a cancellation/adjustment application FOR ANY ALIEN; this wording is not silently collapsed into House's application-category wording or an assumed identity of payer and beneficiary. The ten listed fiscal2025 floors are separate fee events, additional to other authorized fees, with a higher AttorneyGeneral rule amount permitted: adjustment to lawful permanent residence $1,500; waiver of grounds of inadmissibility $1,050; TPS $500; appeal from an immigration-judge decision $900; appeal from a DHS-officer decision $900; practitioner disciplinary appeal $1,325; motion to reopen or reconsider an immigration-judge or Board of Immigration Appeals decision $900; suspension of deportation application $600; cancellation of removal for the specified permanent-resident category $600; and cancellation/adjustment for the specified nonpermanent-resident category $1,500. Each subsection has fiscal2026-onward July-to-July CPI-U adjustment of its own prior-year fee, with the INCREMENT rounded down to $10, not an automatically exact future price or a sum charged to every alien. The disciplinary appeal payer is a PRACTITIONER filing an appeal of an adjudicating official's decision in a practitioner disciplinary case, not every alien or every attorney. Senate 100054 fiscal year 2025 $3.33 billion DOJ envelope through September 30, 2029 has separate selected EOIR, Byrne/COPS and incarceration purposes; neither all funds nor House earmarks are assigned to one. Senate 100054(2)/(3) drug/prosecution purposes use the shared $3.33 billion fiscal year 2025 envelope through September 30, 2029, without House earmarks. Own listed matters include unlawful voting; full 611 federal-office/exception/nonapplication predicates remain, no generic alien-guilt or new benefit/voting rule. Separate 100055 DOJ Fund. The Attorney General shall use the Fund amounts for grants to eligible States, State agencies, and units of local government, pursuant to their existing statutory authorities, for any of the following purposes. The paragraph 1 purpose is locating and apprehending aliens who have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. The paragraph 2 purpose is collection and analysis of law enforcement investigative information within the United States to counter gang or other criminal activity. The paragraph 3 purpose is investigating and prosecuting crimes committed by aliens within the United States and drug and human trafficking crimes committed within the United States. The paragraph 4 purpose is court operations related to the prosecution of crimes committed by aliens and drug and human trafficking crimes. The paragraph 5 purpose is temporary criminal detention of aliens. The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting aliens described in paragraph (1) within the United States to locations related to the apprehension, detention, and prosecution of such aliens. The paragraph 7 purpose is vehicle maintenance, logistics, transportation, and other support provided to law enforcement agencies by a State agency to enhance the ability to locate and apprehend aliens who have committed crimes under Federal, State, or local law, in addition to being unlawfully present in the United States. Paragraphs (1) and (7) retain their own additional-crime and unlawful-presence requirements; paragraph (6) retains the paragraph (1) person category, its domestic transport limit and its destination purposes. Those requirements are not imported into the other purposes. Temporary criminal detention is distinct from civil immigration detention. Court paragraph (4) prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase; no neighboring location condition is borrowed. Listed conjunctions report the source categories, not a determination that a particular grant must fund both crime categories. Existing statutory authorities do not create new State arrest/removal powers or establish actual crime/status/expense eligibility. Fiscal year 2025 appropriation is not to exceed $3,500,000,000 ($3.5 billion) until September 30, 2028, with qualified and documented expenses. The Attorney General may provide grants to State agencies and units of local government for their expenditures for completed, ongoing, or new activities determined to be eligible for such grant funding that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Amounts made available under this section shall be distributed to more than 1 State. No borrowed January 21 or 2029 date, automatic grant, actual crime/status/detention/hiring/spending or full-package closure. Existing question 46 subsection-scope application is unchanged.

Senate 100051(9)/(10) use the additional fiscal year 2025 $2,055,000,000 DHS envelope through September 30, 2029, in accordance with 235(b)(1)/(c), without House earmarks, House's express 212(a)(2)/(3) grounds wording or regardless-of-presence phrase. Senate 100051(8) and (11) are purposes within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. Neither purpose is a separate earmark for the full account, the ICE account or a House child appropriation. Paragraph (8) funds removal operations for specified unaccompanied alien children, but amounts under this paragraph shall only be used for permitting a specified unaccompanied alien child to withdraw the application for admission of the child pursuant to section 235(a)(4). The Secretary of Homeland Security must determine on a case-by-case basis all three specified-child conditions. First, the child has been found by an immigration officer at a land border or port of entry of the United States and is inadmissible under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Second, the child has not been a victim of severe forms of trafficking in persons, and there is no credible evidence that such child is at risk of being trafficked upon return of the child to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence. Third, the child does not have a fear of returning to the child's country of nationality or country of last habitual residence owing to a credible fear of persecution. The paragraph does not print the House express contiguous-or-non-contiguous-country phrase or an independent-decision finding; neither is silently inserted into its definition. The incorporated unaccompanied-alien-child definition requires no lawful immigration status in the United States and not having attained 18 years of age, together with either no parent or legal guardian in the United States or no parent or legal guardian in the United States available to provide care and physical custody. The complete severe-forms-of-trafficking definition is bound with its own sex-trafficking and labor-or-services alternatives, force/fraud/coercion and under-18 distinctions; no label alone determines a child's eligibility. Paragraph (11) funds criminal and gang checks of defined unaccompanied alien children who are 12 years of age and older, including the examination of such unaccompanied alien children for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings. It prints no separate encountered-by-CBP condition; the House 70116 encounter condition is not imported. Its age-12 floor belongs to this check purpose, not the paragraph (8) withdrawal definition. Examination funding is not a finding that a child belongs to a gang, has committed a crime or is dangerous. Complete material captured pre-vote 235(a)(4) retains discretionary permission to withdraw and depart immediately, not a mandatory withdrawal or removal order. Complete TVPRA 235/1232 retains its own contiguous-child case-by-case trafficking/fear and independent-decision conditions, discretionary withdrawal/return, safe-return conditions, 48-hour screening and failed-or-undetermined-screen transfer, other-child custody pathway and own notification/72-hour-transfer exceptions. Its removal-proceedings, relief/access-to-counsel, placement, suitability and remaining safeguards retain their own scope. Senate funding does not itself establish their repeal, fulfillment or a universal individual return, protection or counsel outcome. Exact application interaction remains separate question 49; House question 43 is preserved independently.

Senate 100051(5) fingerprint and DNA purposes are within the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 Secretary of Homeland Security account through September 30, 2029. Both purposes share the printed circumstance of aliens and alien children entering the United States without a valid visa. Subparagraph (A) funds collecting fingerprints, in accordance with section 262 and subsections (a)(3) and (b) of section 235 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. Subparagraph (B) separately funds collecting DNA, in accordance with sections 235(d) and 287(b) of that Act. These are funding purposes with their own incorporated authorities, not a determination that every alien or child is subject to every collection power or that funded collection actually occurred. Captured 262(a) concerns an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is fourteen years of age or older, has not been registered and fingerprinted under section 1201(b) or section 30 or 31 of the Alien Registration Act, 1940, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer. All those conditions are common to its duty to apply for registration and to be fingerprinted before the expiration of such thirty days. Captured 262(b) separately requires a parent or legal guardian to apply for registration of an alien now or hereafter in the United States who is less than fourteen years of age, has not been registered under those named provisions, and remains in the United States for thirty days or longer, before that period expires. That parent/guardian provision prints registration, not the same under-14 fingerprint duty. Whenever an alien attains his fourteenth birthday in the United States, the separate rule requires in-person registration and fingerprinting within thirty days thereafter. Captured 262(c) retains the Attorney General's discretionary nonimmigrant fingerprint waiver on the basis of reciprocity pursuant to prescribed regulations; no actual waiver is inferred. Complete 235(a)(3) concerns inspection of aliens, including crewmen, who apply for or otherwise seek admission, readmission or transit; it does not itself print a fingerprint command. Complete material 235(b)(1)/(2) screening, exceptions, asylum/fear/interview/review/consultation/detention and contiguous-return conditions remain bound, together with the original favorable-admission challenge. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 renumbers that original challenge from (3) to (4) and inserts the distinct State enforcement (3); the captured 2024 wording is not relabeled as an unamended 2025 subsection. Complete 235(d) retains its own belief-based conveyance search, detention/delivery with the alien-crewmember exception, named oath/evidence powers and subpoena-purpose/court-enforcement conditions. Complete 287(b) retains the designated officer/employee oath/evidence scope and its own knowing-or-willful false-evidence/perjury conditions. Neither cited provision expressly names DNA collection. That literal observation does not resolve whether other law, implementation rules or this funding language supports a proposed collection; question 50 reserves the exact DNA authority/application interaction. Question 51 separately reserves the fingerprint-purpose no-valid-visa circumstance alongside the incorporated registration age/prior-registration/duration/waiver paths and inspection procedures. No statutory repeal, guaranteed discretion outcome, universal biometric collection or actual child/parent/status/registration finding is inferred.

Remaining Senate 100051 purposes (1) through (4), (6), (7) and (12) share the additional $2,055,000,000 fiscal year 2025 appropriation to the Secretary of Homeland Security, available through September 30, 2029. They are purposes within that account, not separate full-envelope earmarks or borrowed ICE/House amounts. The paragraph 1 purpose is hiring and training of additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection agents, and the necessary support staff, to carry out immigration enforcement activities. The paragraph 2 purpose is funding for transportation costs and related costs associated with the departure or removal of aliens. The paragraph 3 purpose is funding for the assignment of Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers to carry out immigration enforcement activities pursuant to sections 103(a) and 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 1357(g)). The paragraph 4 purpose is hiring additional staff and investing the necessary resources to enhance screening and vetting of all aliens seeking entry into United States, consistent with section 212 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1182), or intending to remain in the United States, consistent with section 237 of such Act (8 U.S.C. 1227). The paragraph 6 purpose is transporting and facilitating the return, pursuant to section 235(b)(2)(C) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(C)), of aliens arriving from contiguous territory. The paragraph 7 purpose is funding for State and local participation in homeland security efforts for purposes of: ending the presence of criminal gangs and criminal organizations throughout the United States; addressing crime and public safety threats; combating human smuggling and trafficking networks throughout the United States; supporting immigration enforcement activities; and providing reimbursement for State and local participation in such efforts. The paragraph 12 purpose is information technology investments to support immigration purposes, including improvements to fee and revenue collections. The entry and intended-remain screening categories retain their own section 212 and section 237 references. The State/local participation list retains all five own purposes, including its own throughout-the-United-States phrases. It does not borrow the reimbursement fund's crime-plus-unlawful-presence category or domestic transport restriction. The general departure/removal transportation purpose prints no separate within-the-United-States phrase. The assignment list retains Department of Homeland Security employees and State officers pursuant to both printed statutory references, not authority for any State employee to exercise all Federal powers. The printed purpose lists do not determine that a particular expenditure must fulfill every listed category. Fee and revenue collection IT is not a new fee, fine or penalty charge. Complete captured 103(a) retains its named agency roles, regulatory/delegation powers, consents and other conditions. In captured 103(a)(10), the Attorney General may authorize a State or local law enforcement officer to perform or exercise any of the powers, privileges, or duties conferred or imposed by this chapter or regulations issued thereunder upon officers or employees of the Service only in the event of the Attorney General's determination that an actual or imminent mass influx of aliens arriving off the coast of the United States, or near a land border, presents urgent circumstances requiring an immediate Federal response, and with the consent of the head of the department, agency, or establishment under whose jurisdiction the individual is serving. The captured event-specific authorization does not establish general unconditioned State power. Previously bound full 287(g) agreement qualifications, training, written powers/duration, Federal direction/supervision, voluntary/communication/cooperation and expense/employment/liability distinctions remain unchanged. Complete captured section 212(a) grounds and remaining operative section 212 authorities retain their own standards, exceptions, discretionary waivers and conditional notice rules, not an every-alien crime finding or guaranteed notice/waiver. January 29, 2025 Public Law 119-1 replaces the original Attorney General references in 212(d)(5) with Secretary of Homeland Security and adds the distinct State enforcement route. Original captured 2024 words are preserved with that amending law, not relabeled as the complete unamended 2025 section. Complete captured section 237 retains distinct deportability grounds, actual conviction/knowledge/timing or other own requirements, exceptions/waivers, special nonimmigrant and SIJ boundaries and conditional administrative stays; screening funding does not determine an individual inadmissible, deportable or criminal. The contiguous-return purpose is pursuant to 235(b)(2)(C). The captured 235(b)(2)(C) return authority concerns an applicant for admission whom the examining immigration officer determines is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, arriving on land (whether or not at a designated port of arrival) from a foreign territory contiguous to the United States. The Attorney General may return that alien to that territory pending a proceeding under section 1229a. The captured parent exceptions for a crewman, an alien to whom paragraph (1) applies, and a stowaway remain. Discretionary return is not a final removal order or universal cross-border return duty. Complete captured 240 proceedings retain judge/charge/exclusive-procedure exceptions, own representation and evidence/examination limits, burdens, decision/appeal, motion and notice/deadline/stay rules. No guaranteed relief, government-paid counsel or individual hearing/return result is inferred. Other H.R.1 immigration components and separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

The Senate 90005(b) State Border Security Reinforcement Fund is a distinct DHS fund. Its complete selected operative clauses are retained below. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 1: There is established, in the Department of Homeland Security, a fund to be known as the ``State Border Security Reinforcement Fund.'' Senate 90005(b) paragraph 2: The Secretary of Homeland Security shall use amounts appropriated or otherwise made available for the Fund for grants to eligible States and units of local government for any of the following purposes: Senate 90005(b) purpose A: Construction or installation of a border wall, border fencing or other barrier, or buoys along the southern border of the United States, which may include planning, procurement of materials, and personnel costs related to such construction or installation. Senate 90005(b) purpose B: Any work necessary to prepare the ground at or near land borders to allow construction and maintenance of a border wall or other barrier fencing. Senate 90005(b) purpose C: Detection and interdiction of illicit substances and aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States and have committed a crime under Federal, State, or local law, and transfer or referral of such aliens to the Department of Homeland Security as provided by law. Senate 90005(b) purpose D: Relocation of aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States from small population centers to other domestic locations. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 3: In addition to amounts otherwise available for the purposes described in paragraph (2), there is appropriated for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to the Department of Homeland Security for the State Border Security Reinforcement Fund established by paragraph (1), $10,000,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2034, for qualified expenses for such purposes. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 4: The Secretary of Homeland Security may provide grants from the fund established by paragraph (1) to State agencies and units of local governments for expenditures made for completed, ongoing, or new activities, in accordance with law, that occurred on or after January 20, 2021. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 5: Each State desiring to apply for a grant under this subsection shall submit an application to the Secretary containing such information in support of the application as the Secretary may require. The Secretary shall require that each State include in its application the purposes for which the State seeks the funds and a description of how the State plans to allocate the funds. The Secretary shall begin to accept applications not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this Act. Senate 90005(b) paragraph 6: Nothing in this subsection shall authorize any State or local government to exercise immigration or border security authorities reserved exclusively to the Federal Government under the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq.) or the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). The Federal Emergency Management Agency may use not more than 1 percent of the funds made available under this subsection for the purpose of administering grants provided for in this section. The paragraph (2)(C) alien category retains both unlawful entry and commission of a crime under Federal, State, or local law; those alien predicates do not classify illicit substances. Transfer or referral remains as provided by law. Paragraph (2)(D) instead concerns unlawful presence and relocation from small population centers to other domestic locations; it does not borrow the crime or unlawful-entry predicates from (C), or authorize an international return. Only (A) specifies the southern border; (B) says at or near land borders. The paragraph (2) eligible-State/local-unit grant purpose rule and paragraph (4) discretionary State-agency/local-government expenditure rule remain distinct. The paragraph (5) application obligations name each State; no additional local-government obligation is inferred. The 90-day clause concerns when the Secretary must begin accepting applications, not an applicant deadline or a finding that applications are open. The paragraph (6) construction rule preserves exclusively Federal authorities without deciding which actual functions or expenditures fall within that reservation. The FEMA administration ceiling is discretionary, no more than 1 percent of funds under this subsection for grants in this section; its two scope words remain distinct. This is not an actual award, expenditure, eligibility, individual status/crime, relocation, power delegation or reimbursement determination. House reimbursement amounts, availability, January 21 date and duplicate-reimbursement restriction are not imported. Other package components and the 51 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected Senate 90005(a) funding and its own program context follow. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 1: In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, to remain available until September 30, 2029, to be administered under the State Homeland Security Grant Program authorized under section 2004 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605), to enhance State, local, and Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements, and other activities-- Senate 90005(a) purpose A: $500,000,000 for State and local capabilities to detect, identify, track, or monitor threats from unmanned aircraft systems (as such term is defined in section 44801 of title 49, United States Code), consistent with titles 18 and 49 of the United States Code; Senate 90005(a) purpose B: $625,000,000 for security and other costs related to the 2026 FIFA World Cup; Senate 90005(a) purpose C: $1,000,000,000 for security, planning, and other costs related to the 2028 Olympics; and Senate 90005(a) purpose D: $450,000,000 for the Operation Stonegarden Grant Program. Senate 90005(a) paragraph 2: None of the funds made available under subparagraph (B) or (C) of paragraph (1) shall be subject to the requirements of section 2004(e)(1) or section 2008(a)(12) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 605(e)(1), 609(a)(12)). The pre-vote fiscal year 2024 DHS/FEMA HSGP notice reproduced on Hawaii's official host describes Operation Stonegarden as supporting enhanced cooperation and coordination among CBP, USBP, and Federal, State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies to improve overall border security. It funds joint border-security efforts along routes of ingress and egress to and from international borders, including travel corridors in States bordering Mexico and Canada and States and territories with international water borders. In that notice, those State, local, Tribal and territorial law enforcement agencies use their inherent law enforcement authorities and receive no additional authority from participating in Stonegarden. This is dated program-purpose context, not a new power conferred by the Senate appropriation or a complete 2025 eligibility rule. The additional fiscal year 2025 appropriation names FEMA Administrator, availability until September 30, 2029, administration under the State Homeland Security Grant Program in 6 U.S.C. 605, and State/local/Tribal security through grants, contracts, cooperative agreements and other activities. The Stonegarden purpose is $450,000,000 within that administration provision. The drone-threat, FIFA and Olympics purposes retain their own printed objects and amounts as adjacent context; those purposes alone do not establish an immigration purpose. The exemption from 605(e)(1) minimum allocation and 609(a)(12) grant-administration expense cap expressly names only FIFA paragraph (1)(B) and Olympics paragraph (1)(C); no exemption for Stonegarden paragraph (1)(D) or drone paragraph (1)(A) is inferred. Captured 605(e)(1) retains its State and named-territory minimum-allocation branches, own fiscal-year denominators and percentages; captured 609(a)(12) permits expenses directly related to grant administration except that such expenses may not exceed 3 percent of the grant amount. Neither this cap nor those minima are reclassified as the separate 90005(b) FEMA one-percent ceiling. Complete captured 603, 605 and 609 retain their own program relationships, application/distribution/multistate rules, permitted-use and personnel/construction/recreation restrictions, waivers, reimbursement, transfers and equipment requirements. Their application to a particular 2025 Stonegarden award, including interaction with the dated 2024 notice's separate HSGP components and conditions, is reserved as question 52. No 2024 funding amount, application deadline, performance period, subrecipient tier or approval automatically governs this new appropriation. No particular State/local/Tribal award, entitlement, expenditure, additional law-enforcement power or individual status result is inferred. Other package components and all previously reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected exact Senate 70119 death/disability loan-discharge income-exclusion and SSN provisions follow. Senate 70119 exclusion grounds: In the case of an individual, gross income does not include any amount which (but for this subsection) would be includible in gross income for such taxable year by reason of the discharge (in whole or in part) of any loan described in subparagraph (B), if such discharge was-- (i) pursuant to subsection (a) or (d) of section 437 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 or the parallel benefit under part D of title IV of such Act (relating to the repayment of loan liability), (ii) pursuant to section 464(c)(1)(F) of such Act, or (iii) otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. Senate 70119 loan categories: A loan is described in this subparagraph if such loan is-- (i) a student loan (as defined in paragraph (2)), or (ii) a private education loan (as defined in section 140(a) of the Consumer Credit Protection Act (15 U.S.C. 1650(a)). Senate 70119 identification and own marital rules: (i) In general.--Subparagraph (A) shall not apply with respect to any discharge during any taxable year unless the taxpayer includes the taxpayer's social security number on the return of tax for such taxable year. (ii) Social security number.--For purposes of this subparagraph, the term `social security number' has the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7).. Senate 70119 math-error amendment: Section 6213(g)(2), as amended by this Act, is further amended by striking and at the end of subparagraph (V), by striking the period at the end of subparagraph (W) and inserting , and, and by inserting after subparagraph (W) the following new subparagraph: (X) an omission of a correct social security number required under section 108(f)(5)(C) (relating to discharges on account of death or disability).. Senate 70119 discharge-date applicability: The amendments made by this section shall apply to discharges after December 31, 2025. Each version replaces only 108(f)(5) with the printed exclusion, not all of section 108 or every student-loan tax rule. The original 2024 (5) instead covers its defined discharge categories after December 31, 2020 and before January 1, 2026; the candidate does not silently extend that entire temporary rule unchanged. The common requirement that the discharged loan meet new subparagraph (B) applies across all three ground alternatives. Interaction of that gate, complete loan definitions and the parent-borrower 437(d) reference is reserved as question 55; no blanket conclusion that every HEA discharge qualifies for tax exclusion. Original (f)(1) service-conditioned discharge and (4) named repayment-program exclusions remain separate. New loan categories retain full 108(f)(2) student-loan definition and entire 140(a) private-education definitions, including actual (a)(8) private loan, own private-lender and expense meanings and excluded credit/mortgage categories. This does not mean every education-related debt qualifies. The three exclusion-ground alternatives remain separate: the first two use their specified HEA discharge paths, while only the third prints otherwise discharged on account of death or total and permanent disability of the student. A parent borrower is not silently equated to the student. Full 437(a) retains qualifying loans, death/disability determinations, safeguards, conditional reinstatement, VA documentation and own income-monitoring/approval/opt-out/update rules; 437(d) separately addresses a parent loan when the student dies. Captured 464(c)(1)(F) retains loan-fund agreement scope, borrower death, regulated permanent/total disability, the medically determinable substantial-gainful-activity alternative with its own duration/death tests, and VA unemployability due to service-connected disability. Part D parallel benefit is retained with complete captured 455 and its unless-otherwise-specified limitation, not a universal cancellation promise. Tax exclusion after a qualifying discharge is distinct from authority to cancel a loan. Both versions define the SSN by 24(h)(7), with their own same-bill amended definition and previously bound SSA issuance authority: citizen or the specified authorization route, and issuance before the return due date, not a bare identification number or a citizen-only rule. No child-credit amount or qualifying-child requirement is imported into the loan exclusion. Math-error treatment retains the existing notice and conditional abatement/deficiency procedure, including the 60-day abatement-request path; it is not a fraud finding or actual assessment. The effective date is discharges after December 31, 2025, not taxable years beginning after that date. No individual exclusion, discharge, marital status, SSA-number validity or return result is inferred. Senate requires the taxpayer SSN on the return and does not print the House conditional-spouse requirement or similar-32(d) addition. Those House clauses are not borrowed. Senate further amends the as-amended math-error list by adding (X), not House (W). House application question 54 is not treated as a settled Senate marital rule. Other H.R.1 components and all separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.

Selected exact Senate account and separate pilot eligibility clauses follow. Senate 70204 IRA treatment with own exceptions: Except as provided in this section or under regulations or guidance established by the Secretary, a Trump account shall be treated for purposes of this title in the same manner as an individual retirement account under section 408(a). Senate 70204 account establishment and instrument: The term `Trump account' means an individual retirement account (as defined in section 408(a)) which is not designated as a Roth IRA and which meets the following requirements: (A) The account-- (i) is created or organized by the Secretary for the exclusive benefit of an eligible individual or such eligible individual's beneficiaries, or (ii) is-- (I) created or organized in the United States for the exclusive benefit of an individual who has not attained the age of 18 before the end of the calendar year, or such individual's beneficiaries, and (II) funded by a qualified rollover contribution. (B) The account is designated (in such manner as the Secretary shall prescribe) at the time of the establishment of the account as a Trump account. (C) The written governing instrument creating the account meets the following requirements: (i) No contribution will be accepted-- (I) before the date that is 12 months after the date of the enactment of this section, or (II) in the case of a contribution made in any calendar year before the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18, if such contribution would result in aggregate contributions (other than exempt contributions) for such calendar year in excess of the contribution limit specified in subsection (c)(2)(A). (ii) Except as provided in subsection (d), no distribution will be allowed before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. (iii) No part of the account funds will be invested in any asset other than an eligible investment during any period before the first day of the calendar year in which the account beneficiary attains age 18. Senate 70204 eligible individual and reciprocal election paths: The term `eligible individual' means any individual-- (A) who has not attained the age of 18 before the close of the calendar year in which the election under subparagraph (C) is made, (B) for whom a social security number (within the meaning of section 24(h)(7)) has been issued before the date on which an election under subsection (C) is made, and (C) for whom-- (i) an election is made under this subparagraph by the Secretary if the Secretary determines (based on information available to the Secretary from tax returns or otherwise) that such individual meets the requirements of subparagraphs (A) and (B) and no prior election has been made for such individual under clause (ii), or (ii) an election is made under this subparagraph by a person other than the Secretary (at such time and in such manner as the Secretary may prescribe) for the establishment of a Trump account if no prior election has been made for such individual under clause (i). Senate 70204 account beneficiary: The term `account beneficiary' means the individual on whose behalf the Trump account was established. Senate 70204 full-balance account rollover: For purposes of this section, the term `qualified rollover contribution' means an amount which is paid in a direct trustee-to-trustee transfer from a Trump account maintained for the benefit of the account beneficiary to a Trump account maintained for such beneficiary, but only if the amount of such payment is equal to the entire balance of the Trump account from which the payment is made. Senate 70204 elected child payment: In the case of an individual who makes an election under this section with respect to an eligible child of the individual, such eligible child shall be treated as making a payment against the tax imposed by subtitle A (for the taxable year for which the election was made) in an amount equal to $1,000. Senate 70204 refund to child account: The amount treated as a payment under subsection (a) shall be paid by the Secretary to the Trump account with respect to which such eligible child is the account beneficiary. Senate 70204 pilot birth window, no prior election and citizenship: For purposes of this section, the term `eligible child' means a qualifying child (as defined in section 152(c))-- (1) who is born after December 31, 2024, and before January 1, 2029, (2) with respect to whom no prior election has been made under this section by such individual or any other individual, and (3) who is a United States citizen. Senate 70204 pilot election administration: An election under this section shall be made at such time and in such manner as the Secretary shall provide. Senate 70204 pilot child identification and election-date definition: (1) In general.--This section shall not apply to any taxpayer unless such individual includes with the election made under this section the social security number of the eligible child with respect to whom the election is made. Senate 70201 deduction and reporting gate: There shall be allowed as a deduction an amount equal to the qualified tips received during the taxable year that are included on statements furnished to the individual pursuant to section 6041(d)(3), 6041A(e)(3), 6050W(f)(2), or 6051(a)(18), or reported by the taxpayer on Form 4137 (or successor). Senate 70201 amount and income limits: (1) In general.--The amount allowed as a deduction under this section for any taxable year shall not exceed $25,000. (2) Limitation based on adjusted gross income.-- (A) In general.--The amount allowable as a deduction under subsection (a) (after application of paragraph (1)) shall be reduced (but not below zero) by $100 for each $1,000 by which the taxpayer's modified adjusted gross income exceeds $150,000 ($300,000 in the case of a joint return). (B) Modified adjusted gross income.--For purposes of this paragraph, the term `modified adjusted gross income' means the adjusted gross income of the taxpayer for the taxable year increased by any amount excluded from gross income under section 911, 931, or 933. Senate 70201 non-employee business-income limit: In the case of qualified tips received by an individual during any taxable year in the course of a trade or business (other than the trade or business of performing services as an employee) of such individual, such qualified tips shall be taken into account under subsection (a) only to the extent that the gross income for the taxpayer from such trade or business for such taxable year (including such qualified tips) exceeds the sum of the deductions (other than the deduction allowed under this section) allocable to the trade or business in which such qualified tips are received by the individual for such taxable year. Senate 70201 qualified-tip conditions: For purposes of this section-- (1) In general.--The term `qualified tips' means cash tips received by an individual in an occupation which customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024, as provided by the Secretary. (2) Exclusions.--Such term shall not include any amount received by an individual unless-- (A) such amount is paid voluntarily without any consequence in the event of nonpayment, is not the subject of negotiation, and is determined by the payor, (B) the trade or business in the course of which the individual receives such amount is not a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2)), and (C) such other requirements as may be established by the Secretary in regulations or other guidance are satisfied. For purposes of subparagraph (B), in the case of an individual receiving tips in the trade or business of performing services as an employee, such individual shall be treated as receiving tips in the course of a trade or business which is a specified service trade or business if the trade or business of the employer is a specified service trade or business. (3) Cash tips.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `cash tips' includes tips received from customers that are paid in cash or charged and, in the case of an employee, tips received under any tip-sharing arrangement. Senate 70201 identification: (1) In general.--No deduction shall be allowed under this section unless the taxpayer includes on the return of tax for the taxable year such individual's social security number. (2) Social security number defined.--For purposes of paragraph (1), the term `social security number' shall have the meaning given such term in section 24(h)(7). Senate 70201 own married-individual joint-return rule: If the taxpayer is a married individual (within the meaning of section 7703), this section shall apply only if the taxpayer and the taxpayer's spouse file a joint return for the taxable year. Selected exact Senate 87001 ORR sponsor-vetting funding and own purpose boundaries follow. Senate 87001 ORR appropriation: (a) Appropriation.--In addition to amounts otherwise available, there is appropriated to the Office of Refugee Resettlement for fiscal year 2025, out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated, $300,000,000, to remain available until September 30, 2028, for the purposes described in subsection (b). Senate 87001 exclusive funded-purpose boundary: (b) Use of Funds.--The funds made available under subsection (a) may only be used for the Office of Refugee Resettlement to support costs associated with-- Senate 87001 background-check purpose and required contents: (1) background checks on potential sponsors, which shall include-- (A) the name of the potential sponsor and of all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (B) the social security number or tax payer identification number of the potential sponsor and of all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (C) the date of birth of the potential sponsor and of all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (D) the validated location of the residence at which the unaccompanied alien child will be placed; (E) an in-person or virtual interview with, and suitability study concerning, the potential sponsor and all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; (F) contact information for the potential sponsor and for all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household; and (G) the results of all background and criminal records checks for the potential sponsor and for all adult residents of the potential sponsor's household, which shall include, at a minimum, an investigation of the public records sex offender registry, a public records background check, and a national criminal history check based on fingerprints; Senate 87001 home-study purpose: (2) home studies of potential sponsors of unaccompanied alien children; Senate 87001 child examination and covering purpose: (3) determining whether an unaccompanied alien child poses a danger to self or others by conducting an examination of the unaccompanied alien child for gang-related tattoos and other gang-related markings and covering such tattoos or markings while the child is in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement; Senate 87001 data-system purpose: (4) data systems improvement and sharing that supports the health, safety, and well being of unaccompanied alien children by determining the appropriateness of potential sponsors of unaccompanied alien children and of adults residing in the household of the potential sponsor and by assisting with the identification and investigation of child labor exploitation and child trafficking; and Senate 87001 State child-welfare coordination purpose: (5) coordinating and communicating with State child welfare agencies regarding the placement of unaccompanied alien children in such States by the Office of Refugee Resettlement. Senate 87001 own sponsor and child definitions: (c) Definitions.--In this section: (1) Potential sponsor.--The term potential sponsor means an individual or entity who applies for the custody of an unaccompanied alien child. (2) Unaccompanied alien child.--The term unaccompanied alien child has the meaning given such term in section 462(g) of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 279(g)). Original 279(g) incorporated category boundary: The incorporated unaccompanied alien child category requires all three conditions: has no lawful immigration status in the United States; has not attained 18 years of age; and either there is no parent or legal guardian in the United States, or no parent or legal guardian in the United States is available to provide care and physical custody. Placement means the placement of an unaccompanied alien child in either a detention facility or an alternative to such a facility. Age alone does not establish this category, and availability for care and physical custody is retained. Original 1232(c)(2)-(3) placement and suitability protections: (2) Safe and secure placements (A) Minors in department of health and human services custody Subject to section 279(b)(2) of title 6, an unaccompanied alien child in the custody of the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall be promptly placed in the least restrictive setting that is in the best interest of the child. In making such placements, the Secretary may consider danger to self, danger to the community, and risk of flight. Placement of child trafficking victims may include placement in an Unaccompanied Refugee Minor program, pursuant to section 412(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1522(d)), if a suitable family member is not available to provide care. A child shall not be placed in a secure facility absent a determination that the child poses a danger to self or others or has been charged with having committed a criminal offense. The placement of a child in a secure facility shall be reviewed, at a minimum, on a monthly basis, in accordance with procedures prescribed by the Secretary, to determine if such placement remains warranted. (B) Aliens transferred from Department of Health and Human Services to Department of Homeland Security custody If a minor described in subparagraph (A) reaches 18 years of age and is transferred to the custody of the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Secretary shall consider placement in the least restrictive setting available after taking into account the alien's danger to self, danger to the community, and risk of flight. Such aliens shall be eligible to participate in alternative to detention programs, utilizing a continuum of alternatives based on the alien's need for supervision, which may include placement of the alien with an individual or an organizational sponsor, or in a supervised group home. (3) Safety and suitability assessments (A) In general Subject to the requirements of subparagraph (B), an unaccompanied alien child may not be placed with a person or entity unless the Secretary of Health and Human Services makes a determination that the proposed custodian is capable of providing for the child's physical and mental well-being. Such determination shall, at a minimum, include verification of the custodian's identity and relationship to the child, if any, as well as an independent finding that the individual has not engaged in any activity that would indicate a potential risk to the child. (B) Home studies Before placing the child with an individual, the Secretary of Health and Human Services shall determine whether a home study is first necessary. A home study shall be conducted for a child who is a victim of a severe form of trafficking in persons, a special needs child with a disability (as defined in section 12102 of title 42), a child who has been a victim of physical or sexual abuse under circumstances that indicate that the child's health or welfare has been significantly harmed or threatened, or a child whose proposed sponsor clearly presents a risk of abuse, maltreatment, exploitation, or trafficking to the child based on all available objective evidence. The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall conduct follow-up services, during the pendency of removal proceedings, on children for whom a home study was conducted and is authorized to conduct follow-up services in cases involving children with mental health or other needs who could benefit from ongoing assistance from a social welfare agency. (C) Access to information Not later than 2 weeks after receiving a request from the Secretary of Health and Human Services, the Secretary of Homeland Security shall provide information necessary to conduct suitability assessments from appropriate Federal, State, and local law enforcement and immigration databases. Senate adds $300 million to ORR for fiscal year 2025, available until September 30, 2028; this is a separate actor/account/date from DHS/ICE funds, not an actual expenditure, placement, screening finding or universal detention mandate. Funds may only support the five printed purpose categories. The background-check purpose shall include all seven items for their own named sponsor/household subjects; retain social security number or tax payer identification number as alternatives, in-person or virtual interview as alternatives, suitability study and all adult residents, and minimum fingerprint-based national criminal history/public-record/sex-offender checks. Do not turn this appropriation into a new universal sponsor citizenship or work-authorized-SSN condition. The child examination purpose has no printed age-12 floor, no CBP-encounter requirement, and covers tattoos or markings while the child is in ORR care; House 70116/70117 conditions are not imported. An examination purpose does not itself establish gang affiliation or danger, and the data-sharing child-labor/trafficking purposes do not establish actual exploitation findings. Potential sponsor expressly includes an individual or entity who applies for custody. The existing full 279 and 1232(c) authorities remain bound with category, placement, suitability, home-study and counsel/advocate protections; this funding is not first-ever placement vetting authority or an implicit repeal of child-protection rules. Exact background-check/use-of-funds conditions are represented as funding-purpose conditions, not a fabricated standalone universal placement deadline or verified practice. Specific protocol, actual placement and compliance/outcome application remain outside this literal candidate. Other H.R.1 component research and the 61 separately reserved application questions remain unfinished.
